matterOverview.title: Arun Mehta vs. Sunrise Properties — Security Deposit Refund

factsSummary: Arun Mehta rented an apartment from Sunrise Properties under a 24-month lease agreement ending July 2025. He paid a security deposit of ₹1,20,000. Upon vacating after the lease expiry, he requested the deposit refund as per the lease terms. The landlord refused, citing vague 'damages to the property' without providing any inspection report, photographs, or repair bills. The tenant documented the move-out condition with timestamped photographs showing the property in good condition. A legal notice was sent on 15 August 2025 demanding the refund, which was ignored.
applicableProvisions: Section 43 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 — Recovery of possession and deposit refund
Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract

precedents.title: Mohd. Ahmed vs. Nizamuddin (2021)
precedents.summary: Landlord withheld security deposit claiming damages without providing any inspection report. The tenant had photographic evidence of the property condition at move-out.

precedents.title: Kailash Sharma vs. Rameshwar Properties (2023)
precedents.summary: Consumer complaint against builder for wrongful withholding of security deposit after lease expiry. Commission held that deposit must be refunded within 45 days of vacating.

favorableFactors: Clear contractual right to deposit refund under signed lease
Tenant fulfilled all lease obligations including full notice period
Move-out photographs directly contradict damage claim
Landlord failed to provide inspection report or repair invoices
Legal notice properly served and acknowledged
unfavorableFactors: Minor disagreement possible on exact refund amount
missingEvidence: Landlord's inspection report (landlord refused to provide)

Obtain written statement from building security about move-out condition

matterOverview.title: Neha Kapoor vs. Vikram Singh — Unpaid Personal Loan Recovery

factsSummary: Neha Kapoor lent ₹5,00,000 to her friend Vikram Singh on 20 January 2025 for his business expansion. A promissory note was signed by the defendant. The defendant made two monthly repayments of ₹25,000 each via bank transfer in February and March 2025, then stopped. When the plaintiff demanded repayment, the defendant claimed the amount was a 'gift' and not a loan. The promissory note exists but no independent witnesses were present during the transaction. WhatsApp messages show the defendant acknowledging the debt initially but later changing his stance.
applicableProvisions: Section 4 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Promissory note definition and enforceability
Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Promise in writing and registered

precedents.title: Sundaram Finance vs. R. S. Iyer (2020)
precedents.summary: Dispute over personal loan where borrower claimed funds were an unconditional gift. Court held that contemporaneous documentation and subsequent conduct determines the nature of transaction.

precedents.title: Meenakshi vs. Rajesh Kumar (2022)
precedents.summary: Friend-to-friend loan dispute where lender had only bank transfer proof but no written agreement. Supreme Court held that bank transfer alone does not prove a loan.

favorableFactors: Signed promissory note establishes acknowledgment of debt
Bank transfer proves funds were disbursed
Partial repayments are inconsistent with 'gift' claim
WhatsApp messages show defendant acknowledging debt initially
unfavorableFactors: Gift vs loan dispute creates material factual dispute
No independent witnesses to the transaction
Unregistered promissory note may face evidentiary challenges
missingEvidence: Signed loan agreement beyond promissory note

simulationFeedback.overallPerformance: Moderate case with some supporting documentation but significant credibility gaps
simulationFeedback.strongestPoint: Partial repayments are strong evidence that defendant recognised the debt
simulationFeedback.weakestPoint: No independent witness to the loan transaction weakens credibility
judgeConcerns: Why no witness was present during the loan transaction
Inconsistency between WhatsApp messages — why did defendant change stance?
suggestedImprovements: Seek discovery of defendant's bank statements to show use of funds
Obtain affidavit from mutual friend about conversations overheard
Compile complete WhatsApp chat history without gaps

nextSteps: Gather any additional written communication acknowledging the loan
Identify any other individuals defendant may have told about the loan
Consider recording a contemporaneous note of the loan conversation
File civil suit for recovery before Civil Judge (Junior Division), Pune

matterOverview.title: Ravi Desai vs. Apex Constructions — Breach of Service Contract

factsSummary: Ravi Desai, an interior designer, verbally agreed with Apex Constructions to provide design and project management services for a commercial office space. The scope of work was discussed informally over meetings and WhatsApp messages. No written contract was signed. The plaintiff provided initial designs, vendor coordination, and site supervision over 6 weeks. A cost estimate of ₹3,50,000 was shared via WhatsApp. The defendant made an initial payment of ₹50,000 but stopped payments midway, claiming the work was substandard and incomplete. The scope, timeline, and quality standards were never formally documented.
applicableProvisions: Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — What agreements are contracts
Section 36 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Effect of failure to perform at fixed time

precedents.title: B. S. Patel vs. Gujarat Builders (2021)
precedents.summary: Service provider claimed payment based on oral contract for construction supervision services. Court held that without written terms, the scope, timeline, and quality standards cannot be objectively determined.

precedents.title: S. S. International vs. M/s Royal Constructions (2023)
precedents.summary: Dispute over professional consultancy services where terms were agreed via email and WhatsApp. Supreme Court held that while electronic communications can constitute a contract, vague terms cannot be enforced.

favorableFactors: Initial payment of ₹50,000 indicates some work was accepted
WhatsApp messages show defendant approved initial designs
unfavorableFactors: Scope of work not formally defined
Defendant has counterclaim for substandard work

simulationFeedback.overallPerformance: Challenging case with significant evidentiary gaps
simulationFeedback.strongestPoint: WhatsApp messages show defendant approved designs and made partial payment
simulationFeedback.weakestPoint: No written contract or defined scope — court cannot determine what was promised vs delivered
judgeConcerns: Why was no written agreement executed for a professional engagement of this value?
How can the court determine what work was actually promised?
suggestedImprovements: Attempt mediation to negotiate a settlement
If proceeding, focus claim on quantum meruit rather than breach of contract
Obtain character testimony about industry practice for similar engagements

nextSteps: Attempt settlement or mediation before litigation
If litigation is necessary, file under the principle of quantum meruit for work actually performed
Obtain independent valuation of work completed
Strongly consider engaging a lawyer experienced in contract disputes before filing
